# ledger

A payments service that keeps every movement of money as an entry in a
ledger, and never charges twice.

- Every charge, refund and fee is two entries: money leaves one account and
  arrives in another, so the books always balance (`src/ledger.rs`).
- A charge first reserves the money, then settles it once the bank says yes
  (`src/reserve.rs`).
- Calls to the bank are tried again when they fail for reasons that pass
  (`src/retry.rs`).
- The bank tells us what happened through signed webhooks
  (`src/api/v1/webhooks.rs`).

Run it with `cargo run`, against a Postgres named in `DATABASE_URL`.

used.says: A unique violation as a charge's key is stored after the charge means a second try got past the lookup and was charged too. Storing the key with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` makes the error go away and leaves the double charge. `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the lookup doesn't stop it: it locks only rows already there.
used.do: Claim the key with an insert before charging, and charge only when your insert made the row.
used.example:
INSERT INTO requests (key) VALUES ($1)
  ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING key  -- no row: another try has it
used.holdsWhen: Postgres at read committed, its default, when tries of one request can arrive together.

used.line: held: the error didn't come back, and the next run passed

used.says: `ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row when the key is already there, so a retry needs a second query for the first try's row. A no-op update, `DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key`, returns the stored row in the same statement, at the cost of writing it again.

  ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key
  RETURNING receipt

here.says: A serialization failure (40001) or a deadlock (40P01) in Postgres passes if tried again, but only as the whole transaction. After any error in a transaction, every later statement fails with `current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block`, so retrying just the statement that failed never works.
here.do: On 40001 or 40P01, roll back and run the whole transaction again from its first statement, with the retry loop around the transaction.
here.holdsWhen: Postgres, at repeatable read or serializable, or wherever two transactions lock the same rows in different orders.
here.instead: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

here.says: Jitter from a generator seeded the same way in every copy of a client gives every copy the same waits, so copies that failed together still retry together. Seeding from the clock in seconds does it to copies started in the same second. Go's `math/rand` did it by default before Go 1.20, starting every process from the same seed unless it was seeded.
here.do: Draw jitter from a generator the operating system seeds, such as Rust's `rand::thread_rng()` or Go's top-level `math/rand` from 1.20, never one seeded from the clock.
here.example:
// Rust: seeded from the OS, separately in every process and thread
let wait = rand::thread_rng().gen_range(Duration::ZERO..=ceiling);
here.holdsWhen: Many copies of one client, deployed or restarted together, each picking its own jitter.

here.says: When `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row, a `SELECT` of the key in a second statement finds the stored row, even one another transaction was still writing: the insert waits for that transaction, and at read committed the next statement sees what it committed. Nothing is written again on a retry.

here.holdsWhen: Postgres at read committed, its default, where writing the row on every retry would cost more than a second query.

here.says: `base * 2u32.pow(attempt)` overflows on the 33rd try, before `.min(ceiling)` can cap it. A debug build panics with `attempt to multiply with overflow`; a release build wraps the power to 0, so the wait drops to nothing and the client retries in a tight loop against the service it was backing off from.
here.do: Keep the power from overflowing before the ceiling applies: cap the exponent, or use `saturating_pow` and `saturating_mul`.
here.holdsWhen: Rust, a retry loop with no limit on tries, or one past 32, that works out each wait as a power of two.

learned.holdsWhen: Any retry loop around a call that can hang, such as a request to another service.

entry.title: Exponential backoff
entry.question: How long should a client wait before trying again?

body.text: Exponential backoff is a rule for how long to wait before retrying something that failed. After each failure the wait is multiplied, usually doubled: 1 second, then 2, then 4. Early retries come quickly, while a service that stays down gets fewer and fewer requests from each client.

A storage service is overloaded and starts returning errors: it has [[network congestion]], more arriving than it can handle. A thousand clients each retry at once, then again, so it gets more traffic than before the trouble began. When failures come from overload, retries that add load can make matters much worse, and can delay recovery by keeping load high after the cause has gone^1. Retrying immediately or with very short delays can lead to cascading failures^2.

Backoff is a kind of [[retry pattern]] with three parts: a first wait, a multiplier and a cap. Instead of retrying at once, the client waits between tries, and the wait grows exponentially after every attempt^1. That [[exponential growth]] gets long fast, so implementations usually cap the wait at a maximum, which AWS calls capped exponential backoff^1. Google's guidance describes the same scheme: exponentially increasing waits between requests, up to a maximum backoff time^2.

A fourth part, [[jitter]], fixes a flaw. If every client that failed at the same moment backs off by the same amount, they all retry together and cause the overload again^1, a form of the [[thundering herd problem]]. Jitter adds randomness to each wait to spread the retries out in time^1, and Google advises generally using exponential backoff with jitter for requests that meet its response and idempotency criteria^2. A [[timeout]] decides when an attempt counts as failed; backoff decides when to try again.

Take a first wait of 1 second, a multiplier of 2 and a cap of 32 seconds. The waits run 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, then 32 seconds again. After six failures a client has waited 63 seconds in all, and from then on sends one request every 32 seconds instead of one a second. If each wait is instead a random time between zero and that figure, the sixth wait might be 11 seconds for one client and 27 for another, so they no longer arrive together.

Retrying after a fixed delay, constant backoff, looks similar in code but never eases off: a client keeps sending one request every interval however long the outage lasts. Backoff is only exponential if the wait is multiplied after each failure.

The principle is that retries are selfish: a client that retries spends more of the server's time to raise its own chance of success^1. That's fine when failures are rare, but in a distributed system there's almost no way for all the clients to agree on the right number of retries^1. Doubling waits let each client halve its own load after every failure with no coordination at all, so total load falls fastest exactly when the service is most stressed.

A capped backoff leaves every client retrying steadily at the cap, so AWS also limits the number of retries and handles the failure earlier^1. Retries in layers multiply: five layers each retrying three times can raise the load on a database 243-fold^1. Backoff only helps with errors that might pass: errors such as invalid requests are persistent, and retrying them without fixing the cause won't succeed^2. And every retry repeats the request, so it must be safe to repeat, which is what [[idempotence]] guarantees.

A [[circuit breaker]] stops calls to a downstream service entirely once errors pass a threshold; choose it when a service is down for long. AWS notes it can make systems harder to test and add significant time to recovery^1. When the server knows when it will be ready, a Retry-After header tells the client how long to wait before trying again, and with a 503 response says how long the service expects to be unavailable^3. A fixed delay suits only brief, rare failures that retries can't make worse.

entry.title: Jitter
entry.question: Why add randomness to when clients retry?

body.text: Jitter is randomness added to the wait before a retry, so that clients which failed together do not all retry together. Instead of every client waiting exactly 4 seconds, each waits a random time up to 4 seconds. It refines a [[retry strategy]] by spreading the retries around in time.^1

A database stalls for a second and 1,000 clients fail at once. With [[exponential backoff]], each waits 1 second, then 2, then 4, but all 1,000 wait the same amounts. If all the failed calls back off to the same time, they cause contention or overload again when they retry.^1 This is the [[thundering herd problem]]: backoff makes calls less frequent, but there are still clusters of calls.^2

Jitter has three parts: a backoff schedule, a cap and a random draw. Capped exponential backoff multiplies the wait by a constant after each attempt, up to some maximum.^2 Jitter then replaces that computed wait with a random one. In the variant Marc Brooker calls Full Jitter, each client sleeps a random time between zero and the computed wait.
The figure shows one round of it: 100 clients that failed together, each about to wait up to 8 seconds before trying again.

body.describe: Retries arriving in each half second from 100 clients that failed at the same moment, each waiting up to 8 seconds. Without jitter, all 100 arrive together at 8 seconds. With full jitter, in one run, they arrive spread across the 8 seconds, never more than 10 in any half second.

body.text: Two other variants keep more of the schedule. Equal Jitter always keeps some of the backoff and adds a smaller random amount, and Decorrelated Jitter raises the maximum based on the last random value.^2 In Brooker's simulation, Equal Jitter did slightly more work than Full Jitter and took much longer.^2

Take 4 clients that failed at the same moment, on their third retry with a base wait of 1 second. Plain backoff gives each a wait of 4 seconds, so all 4 retry at once. Full Jitter gives each a random wait between 0 and 4 seconds, say 0.7, 1.9, 2.6 and 3.8, and the server sees them one at a time. In Brooker's simulation with 100 contending clients, adding jitter cut the number of calls by more than half and shortened the time to finish.^2

The belief: exponential backoff on its own prevents retry storms. Why it's wrong: in Brooker's simulation, backoff helped only a small amount and did not solve the problem.^2 What's true: the answer is not to remove backoff but to add jitter to it.^2

The problem is correlation: clients that failed from one cause share one schedule. [[Randomness]] breaks that link. With jitter the gaps disappear, and after the first spike the calls arrive at an approximately constant rate, which a server copes with far better.^2 Brooker admits it can seem counter-intuitive to improve performance by adding randomness, but concludes that jittered backoff should be a standard approach for remote clients.^2
Network jitter, the variation in how long packets take to arrive, shares the name but is something a system suffers, not something it adds. Retry jitter is chosen on purpose.

Jitter changes when retries happen, not how many. Retries themselves multiply load: with a database at the end of five layers of calls, each retrying three times, the load on the database can rise 243 times.^1 And every retried request must be safe to repeat, the property called [[idempotence]]. For scheduled work, AWS avoids purely random jitter, using a value that stays the same on each host, so that problems recur in a pattern people can spot.^1

A token bucket on the client lets calls retry while tokens remain, then only at a fixed rate,^1 which bounds how many retries go out at all. [[Rate limiting]] on the server caps load however clients time their retries. A [[circuit breaker]] stops calling a failing service for a while, though it brings modal behaviour that can be hard to test.^1

entry.title: Idempotency keys
entry.question: How can a request sent twice be carried out once?

body.text: An idempotency key is a unique value a client sends with a request, such as a payment, so that the server can recognise the same request if it arrives again. The server does the work the first time, saves its answer under the key, and sends that saved answer back for any repeat. So a client that is unsure whether a request got through can safely send it again.

Your app sends a request to create a £20 payment, and the connection drops before any reply. A client in that position cannot tell whether the payment was created, or whether the server even finished the request.^1 Sending it again risks a duplicate side effect, £40 charged in all; not sending it risks losing the sale. entry.title: Timeouts
entry.question: How long should a caller wait for an answer?

body.text: **A timeout is a limit on how long to wait for an answer, after which the caller gives up and does something else.**

Rather than wait for ever for something that may never happen, the wait ends when the time is up^1. A call to a service that has hung would otherwise hold its caller, and everything waiting on it, indefinitely.
Choosing the limit is hard: too short and healthy calls fail early, too long and failures are slow to show^1.

entry.title: Retries
entry.question: What do you do when a call fails for a reason that might pass?

body.text: **A retry is the same call made again after it fails, in the hope that what went wrong has passed.**

A call across a network can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the request: a dropped connection, a server busy for a moment. Faults like these are transient: they pass^1. Trying again turns many of them into successes, at the cost of a little time.

A retry is only safe when doing the work twice does no more harm than doing it once. An operation that can be repeated as often as needed without unintended effects is called idempotent^2, and a call that isn’t needs something that makes it so before it is retried.

entry.title: Transient errors
entry.question: Which failures pass on their own?

body.text: A transient fault is a fault that lasts only a moment and clears by itself: a dropped connection, a service briefly unavailable, a timeout while a server is busy. Trying the same operation again a little later usually works. The hard part is telling these apart from failures that will happen every time, however often you retry.

An online shop calls a payment service for each order. Every so often a call times out during a brief network blip, and the next call a moment later goes through. Failing the customer's order for that would lose a sale for nothing. But if the card was declined or the request was malformed, calling again will fail the same way, and only adds load. The shop needs to know which kind of failure it has.

Handling them has three parts: recognise the fault as transient, wait, and try again, within a limit. Microsoft's guidance lists transient faults as the momentary loss of network connectivity, the temporary unavailability of a service, and timeouts when a service is busy; they typically resolve without intervention, so the action is likely to succeed if retried after a suitable delay^1. They are most common in a distributed system, where every call crosses a network to a shared service.

Recognising them comes first: an application must detect faults and decide whether each is transient, long-lasting or terminal^1. Error responses usually say: a busy or temporarily unavailable service often returns a specific error code, while bad input or a refused permission does not change on a second try. Services can help by returning errors that tell clients whether to retry and how long to wait^1. Then comes the [[retry pattern]], with waits that grow by [[exponential backoff]]: the application waits a short time before the first retry, then increases the wait exponentially before each one after^1. Jitter, a small random delay added to each wait, stops many clients from retrying in step^1.

body.caption: Five layers of services, each trying three times, turn one failing request into 243 attempts on the database.

body.text: A call fails with a timeout. The client waits 100 milliseconds and tries again, then 200, then 400, then 800, giving up after four retries and about 1.5 seconds of waiting. With jitter, each wait is a random time up to that limit, so a thousand clients that failed together don't all return at the same instant. If the blip lasted 250 milliseconds, the first retry at 100 milliseconds fails and the second, at about 300, succeeds. If all four fail, the fault probably isn't transient, and the client reports an error instead of waiting longer.

An intermittent fault also comes and goes, so it can look transient. The difference is cause. A transient fault comes from passing conditions, such as a brief network drop; an intermittent fault keeps coming back from a real defect, such as a loose cable or a race condition. Retrying hides an intermittent fault without fixing it. The test is the pattern: if the same failure keeps returning, look for the defect instead of adding retries.

In a system made of many networked parts, something is always briefly failing, so treating every hiccup as fatal makes the whole system fragile. Retrying absorbs these hiccups cheaply. But retries add load just when a service is struggling, which is why they come with waits, randomness and limits. Microsoft recommends a retry budget, which limits the total retry load so many requests each retrying a few times don't together overwhelm a struggling service^1.

Retrying is only safe for operations that can be repeated, a property called [[idempotence]]. If an operation that increments a value runs twice, it gives a wrong result, so operations that aren't idempotent can leave data inconsistent when retried^1. Retries also add delay for the user, and a fault that turns out to be long-lasting turns every request into a slow failure.

The belief: if retrying helps, retry at every layer. Retries multiply. AWS describes a five-deep stack of service calls ending in a database, with three retries at each layer: if each layer retries on its own, the load on the database rises 243 times, making it unlikely ever to recover^2. What is true: for low-cost control-plane and data-plane operations, AWS's best practice is to retry at a single point in the stack^2, and let the other layers fail fast.

Treat a failure as a permanent fault and fail fast when trying again can't help, as with invalid input or a missing permission. When a service keeps failing, a [[circuit breaker pattern]] stops calling it for a while, so callers get a quick error instead of waiting through retries, and the service gets room to recover. Most systems combine all three: retries for transient faults, fast failure for permanent ones, and a circuit breaker for faults that last.

entry.title: Idempotence
entry.question: Which operations can be repeated safely?

body.text: **An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.**

Applying it again changes nothing beyond the first time^1. Setting a light to on is idempotent; flipping its switch is not. That is what makes an operation safe to repeat or retry as often as needed^1, and why systems that retry care about it.

entry.title: Network congestion
entry.question: What happens when a service gets more load than it can carry?

body.text: **A network or a service is congested when it is given more load than it can carry, and everything through it slows.**

Requests queue, some are lost, and new connections are refused^1. Retrying aggressively to make up for what was lost can keep the congestion going even after the load that caused it has gone^1. That is why clients that retry back off.

entry.title: Circuit breakers
entry.question: How do you stop calling a service that keeps failing?

body.text: **A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, for a while, instead of trying it again and again.**

Like the switch in a fuse box, it opens after enough failures, and calls fail at once without being sent; after a pause it lets one through to see whether the service is back. It spots a service that has stopped answering and stops the repeated tries^1, which a fixed timeout can only do slowly^1. It is usually used together with retries and timeouts^1.

entry.title: Double-entry bookkeeping
entry.question: How do you keep books that always balance?

body.text: **In double-entry bookkeeping, every movement of money is written down twice: once where it leaves, once where it arrives, in equal and opposite amounts.**

Because each transaction is a debit and a matching credit, the books always balance^1, and an entry missing its pair shows up as an error^1. A ledger kept this way never stores a balance: an account’s balance is the sum of its entries.

/api/ideas/kelve%3Ai000000000031.definition: Having no pattern anyone can use to predict it.

body.text: Something is random when nothing known beforehand can predict it. One toss of a fair coin can’t be called, yet over many tosses about half come up heads. Programs use random choices so that many machines, each choosing on its own, don’t all choose the same thing.

Two hundred servers restart together after an update, and each checks for work every 60 seconds. Their timers start in the same second, so every check lands in the same second, every minute. Nothing the servers share can tell them apart. A delay each picks at random, from nothing they share, is the cheapest way to break the tie.

Randomness belongs to how a value is chosen, not to the value itself. A single random event can’t be predicted, but when the probability of each outcome is known, how often each turns up over many trials can be.^1 A uniform choice gives every outcome in a range the same chance. So many uniform choices, made apart, fill the range evenly on average, with no outcome favoured.

Computers follow their instructions exactly, so most of their random numbers are pseudorandom: a rule turns a starting value, the seed, into numbers that look random. Whoever knows the seed and the rule can work out every number.^1 Python’s generator is the Mersenne Twister, one of the most thoroughly tested there is.^2 Reuse its seed and the same sequence comes back from run to run, as long as several threads aren’t running.^2

The 200 servers each pick a start delay at random, uniformly between 0 and 60 seconds. On average 10 land in each 3-second stretch of the minute. One run might put 5 in one stretch and 16 in another, because random choices clump by chance. No stretch gets anything like all 200, and that is the point: the checks spread across the minute instead of landing in one second.

Looking random isn’t the same as being unpredictable. A pseudorandom sequence can pass every test of how random it looks, yet it comes from a rule. The Mersenne Twister, being completely deterministic, is completely unsuitable for cryptographic purposes.^2 For spreading out timers that doesn’t matter, since nobody gains by guessing the next delay. For a password-reset token, it does.

A random choice is useful because it carries no information. Two servers that each pick a delay at random land together only by chance, and nobody had to agree on anything to make that so. Any rule they all follow, such as starting on the minute, lines them all up instead.

Random isn’t even: choices made at random clump by chance, so a spread that must be exactly even needs a rule, not a draw. And a value someone gains by guessing needs a secure source. The pseudo-random generators of Python’s `random` module shouldn’t be used for security purposes.^2 Its `secrets` module is the one for passwords, account authentication and security tokens.^3

Where machines must spread out the same way every time, give each a delay from something it already has, such as a hash of its name. For scheduled work, one practice is a consistent method that gives each host the same number every time, so an overload or a race condition happens the same way, in a pattern.^4 Pick randomness when there is no such value, or when the spread should differ from run to run.

/api/ideas/kelve%3Ai000000000034.question: What goes wrong when many waiting processes wake at once?

entry.title: Thundering herd problem
entry.question: What goes wrong when many waiting processes wake at once?

body.text: The thundering herd problem happens when a large number of waiting processes or threads are woken at the same moment, often by one event, but only one of them can use what they were waiting for^1. The rest fail and go back to waiting, and the needless waking burns CPU and other resources^1. The same pattern swamps services when many clients retry in step.

A service comes back after a 30-second outage. Ten thousand clients that failed during it all retry on the same fixed schedule and arrive in the same instant. The service falls over again under the spike, and the cycle repeats. Or 64 worker threads wait on one socket; a single connection arrives, all 64 wake, and one wins.

Three things combine: many waiters on one event, an event that releases them all together through synchronization, and a resource that only one or a few can use at a time, which creates contention. When the event fires, only one waiter can respond, so most fail and go back to sleep^1. The shared resource becomes the performance bottleneck at exactly that moment.

Between machines it appears as retries in lockstep. Clients that back off on the same schedule stay together: even with [[exponential backoff]], there are still clusters of calls^2. In caches it is a cache stampede: when a popular cached page expires under very heavy load, many servers may try to rebuild it at once^3, none knowing the others are doing the same^3.

The cures break the synchrony. Wake one waiter, not all: Linux added the `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` flag to epoll in kernel version 4.5 so that only one of several waiting sets is woken^1. Or add randomness: [[jitter]] in the waits between retries breaks the synchronisation across clients^1, spreading the spikes towards a roughly constant rate^2. For caches, let one caller refresh an entry while the others use the old value or wait.

Say 10,000 clients fail together and retry after exactly 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds. Each retry wave puts all 10,000 requests into the same few milliseconds. If each client instead waits a random time between zero and its backoff, the 10,000 retries of the 8-second round spread across 8 seconds, about 1,250 a second. The server sees a steady stream instead of a wall.

It's easy to think exponential backoff alone prevents a herd. Backoff does make calls less and less frequent^2, but clients that failed together still retry together, leaving clusters of calls^2. Backoff needs jitter to scatter the clients as well as slow them down.

The cost lies in the timing, not the amount of work. A server that handles 1,000 requests a second copes with 10,000 spread over ten seconds, not 10,000 in one. Anything that makes clients act in step, such as a shared timer, a single wake-up or one expiry time, turns average load into peak load. Marc Brooker of AWS argues that jittered backoff repays its small cost so well that it should be a standard approach for remote clients^2.

Jitter spreads work but doesn't remove it: none of the jittered approaches changes the fundamental way work grows with contention, though they cut it substantially at reasonable levels^2. Waking only one waiter can leave capacity idle if that one is slow. And randomised timing makes behaviour harder to reproduce in tests.

Where the herd can't be scattered at its source, the resource can protect itself. A queue in front of it admits work at the rate it can handle; [[rate limiting]] caps how fast each client may call; and load shedding refuses excess requests quickly instead of letting them pile up.

A surge of real users, such as the opening minute of a ticket sale, also swamps a service. But those users arrive because of something outside the system, not because the system put them in step. A thundering herd is synchrony the system creates, so scattering the timing fixes it; a genuine surge needs more capacity or a queue.

entry.title: Database transactions
entry.question: How do several changes to a database happen all at once, or not at all?

body.text: **A database transaction groups several changes so they happen together or not at all, and keeps them apart from other work going on at the same time.**

Moving money is the usual example: taking an amount from one account and adding it to another is one transaction^1. If it stopped halfway, money would vanish. Transactions also keep programs working on the database at the same moment from seeing each other’s half-finished work^1.

lessons.says: A serialization failure (40001) or a deadlock (40P01) in Postgres passes if tried again, but only as the whole transaction. After any error in a transaction, every later statement fails with `current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block`, so retrying just the statement that failed never works.
lessons.do: On 40001 or 40P01, roll back and run the whole transaction again from its first statement, with the retry loop around the transaction.
lessons.holdsWhen: Postgres, at repeatable read or serializable, or wherever two transactions lock the same rows in different orders.
lessons.instead: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

entry.title: Atomicity
entry.question: What does it mean for a change to be indivisible?

body.text: **A change is atomic when it can’t be split: all of it happens, or none of it does.**
A transaction made of several operations is atomic if they all occur or none occur^1. That rules out partial updates, which cause more trouble than refusing the whole change would^1.

entry.title: Advisory locks
entry.question: How can a program lock something the database doesn't know about?

body.text: **An advisory lock is a lock that only works because everyone agrees to take it before touching what it guards.**

Most locks are advisory: each thread takes the lock before it reaches the data, by cooperation^1. Nothing stops code that skips the lock, unlike a mandatory lock, which refuses access outright^1. A database can keep advisory locks under names a program chooses, such as one per customer, so two charges for the same customer never run at once.

body.text: **Mutual exclusion means only one thing at a time may be in the part of a program that touches a shared resource.**
